claim: Twenty-three healthy adult volunteers participated in two combined TMS-rsfMRI experiments, conducted on separate days.
source: Twenty-three healthy adult volunteers participated in two combined TMS-rsfMRI experiments, conducted on separate days.
evidence: Directly stated in the Results section describing the participant sample.

claim: The number of participants was decided based on previous work adopting a similar experimental design (Cocchi et al., 2015; Eldaief et al., 2011).
source: The number of participants was decided based on previous work adopting a similar experimental design (Cocchi et al., 2015; Eldaief et al., 2011).
evidence: Justified by citation to prior studies using similar designs.

claim: After exclusion of data from two participants due to excessive head motion or medication, resting-state data from 21 participants (11 female mean age 27.7, S.D. ± 5.2 years) were analyzed.
source: After exclusion of data from two participants due to excessive head motion or medication, we analyzed resting-state data from 21 of the participants (11 female mean age 27.7, S.D. ± 5.2 years) acquired on a 3T Siemens Trio scanner.
evidence: Explicitly states the final sample size and demographics after exclusions.

claim: Resting-state data were acquired on a 3T Siemens Trio scanner.
source: we analyzed resting-state data from 21 of the participants (11 female mean age 27.7, S.D. ± 5.2 years) acquired on a 3T Siemens Trio scanner.
evidence: Directly states the scanner model used for data acquisition.

claim: Continuous (inhibitory) theta-burst TMS was applied over one of two different cortical regions of interest (ROIs) immediately following an initial rsfMRI session.
source: Immediately following an initial rsfMRI session, continuous (inhibitory) theta-burst TMS (Huang et al., 2005) was applied over one of two different cortical regions of interest (ROIs).
evidence: Describes the experimental protocol with citation to the TMS method.

claim: A repeat rsfMRI scan was acquired from each participant immediately following TMS stimulation.
source: A repeat rsfMRI scan was acquired from each participant immediately following TMS stimulation.
evidence: Directly states the timing of the post-TMS scan.

claim: The first TMS target was the right early visual cortex at the posterior aspect of the medial occipital lobe (MNI centroid x = 25, y = −92, z = −9), corresponding with areas V1/V2.
source: The anatomical locations of the two TMS targets were: (1) Right early visual cortex – the posterior aspect of the medial occipital lobe (MNI centroid x = 25, y = −92, z = −9), corresponding with areas V1/V2
evidence: Explicitly provides anatomical location and coordinates of the first TMS target.

claim: The second TMS target was the right FEF (MNI centroid x = 31 y = −2, z = 47), a brain hub within the frontal cortex.
source: (2) Right FEF (MNI centroid x = 31 y = −2, z = 47) – a brain hub within the frontal cortex (see Materials and methods for target region identification).
evidence: Explicitly provides anatomical location and coordinates of the second TMS target.

claim: During TMS, participants closed their eyes and were seated to ensure a relaxed muscle state.
source: During TMS, participants closed their eyes and were seated to ensure a relaxed muscle state.
evidence: Directly describes the participant state during TMS.

claim: Local stimulation was delivered with participants in a state of rest and in the absence of structured visual input.
source: This procedure ensured that local stimulation was delivered with participants in a state of rest and in the absence of structured visual input.
evidence: Explicitly states the conditions under which TMS was applied.

claim: The order of stimulation of the two cortical sites was counterbalanced across participants.
source: The order of stimulation of the two cortical sites was counterbalanced across participants.
evidence: Directly states the counterbalancing procedure.

claim: Activity within the right occipital seed (V1/V2) was positively correlated with activity in other nodes of the visual network, including the lingual gyri, fusiform gyri, the lateral occipital cortex, and the cuneus bilaterally (Yeo et al., 2011; Power et al., 2011; Gordon et al., 2016) (p<0.05 FWE).
source: As shown in Figure 2, activity within the right occipital seed (V1/V2) was positively correlated with activity in other nodes of the visual network, including the lingual gyri, fusiform gyri, the lateral occipital cortex, and the cuneus bilaterally (Yeo et al., 2011; Power et al., 2011; Gordon et al., 2016) (p<0.05 familywise error corrected at cluster level (FWE), Figure 2a – red).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of baseline connectivity data and referenced to Figure 2, with citations to prior literature.

claim: Activity in the right occipital seed was negatively correlated (anticorrelated) with activity in bilateral FEF, the left supramarginal gyrus, the left inferior post-central gyrus, and the left posterior insula (p<0.05 FWE).
source: By contrast, activity in the same occipital seed was negatively correlated (i.e., anticorrelated) with activity in bilateral FEF, the left supramarginal gyrus, the left inferior post-central gyrus, and the left posterior insula (Figure 2a – blue, p<0.05 FWE).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of baseline connectivity data and referenced to Figure 2a.

claim: In the absence of active visual task demands, interactions between early visual cortex and the right FEF can be anticorrelated (Yeo et al., 2011; Power et al., 2011; Gordon et al., 2016; Ekstrom et al., 2008).
source: These results confirm and extend previous findings by showing that in the absence of active visual task demands, interactions between early visual cortex and the right FEF can be anticorrelated (Yeo et al., 2011; Power et al., 2011; Gordon et al., 2016; Ekstrom et al., 2008).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the data with support from multiple citations.

claim: Neural activity in the right FEF seed was positively correlated with activity in bilateral supplementary motor areas, medial dorsal cingulate, bilateral dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, bilateral superior parietal cortex, and extrastriate visual areas including bilateral precuneus, middle occipital gyri, and inferior temporal gyri (p<0.05 FWE).
source: Neural activity in the right FEF seed was positively correlated with activity in bilateral supplementary motor areas, medial dorsal cingulate, bilateral dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, bilateral superior parietal cortex, and extrastriate visual areas including bilateral precuneus, middle occipital gyri, and inferior temporal gyri (Figure 2b – red, p<0.05 FWE).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of baseline connectivity data and referenced to Figure 2b.

claim: Activity within the right FEF seed was negatively correlated with activity in default mode regions encompassing the medial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate cortex, angular gyrus and bilateral medial temporal gyri (Power et al., 2011) (p<0.05 FWE).
source: Activity within the right FEF seed was also negatively correlated with activity in default mode regions encompassing the medial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate cortex, angular gyrus and bilateral medial temporal gyri (Power et al., 2011) (Figure 2b – blue, p<0.05 FWE).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of baseline connectivity data with citation and reference to Figure 2b.

claim: The FEF is a functional brain hub, with widespread connections to a variety of resting-state networks including the fronto-parietal and default-mode systems (Power et al., 2013; Fornito et al., 2016; van den Heuvel, 2013a, 2013b).
source: Specifically, our results support the idea that the FEF is a functional brain hub, with widespread connections to a variety of resting-state networks including the fronto-parietal and default-mode systems (Power et al., 2013; Fornito et al., 2016; van den Heuvel, 2013a, 2013b).
evidence: Interpretation of results supported by multiple citations.

claim: Inhibitory TMS of right visual cortex (V1/V2) resulted in the emergence of positive correlations between this region and bilateral FEF.
source: Inhibitory TMS of right visual cortex (V1/V2) resulted in the emergence of positive correlations between this region and bilateral FEF (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of pre- vs. post-TMS connectivity data with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: TMS of the visual cortex resulted in the emergence/increase of positive correlations between V1/V2 and extrastriate visual regions including the lingual gyri, the lateral occipital cortex and the parietal cortex (p<0.05 FWE).
source: TMS of the visual cortex also resulted in the emergence/increase of positive correlations between V1/V2 and extrastriate visual regions including the lingual gyri, the lateral occipital cortex and the parietal cortex (p<0.05 FWE; Figure 3a – red, details in Supplementary files 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of pre- vs. post-TMS connectivity data with reference to Figure 3a.

claim: Inhibitory TMS of right FEF resulted in a reduction in positive correlations between the targeted FEF region and visual areas encompassing the bilateral fusiform and occipital gyri.
source: On the other hand, inhibitory TMS of right FEF resulted in a reduction in positive correlations between the targeted FEF region and visual areas encompassing the bilateral fusiform and occipital gyri (Figure 3b – blue, details in Supplementary files 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of pre- vs. post-TMS connectivity data with reference to Figure 3b.

claim: There was a significant correlation between TMS-induced modulation of the amplitude of slow signal fluctuations (ALFF) and TMS-induced changes in functional connectivity for the right FEF (right FEF ROI to left visual cluster r = 0.6, p<0.01; right FEF ROI to right visual cluster r = 0.6, p<0.01).
source: There was a significant correlation between TMS-induced modulation of the amplitude of slow signal fluctuations (ALFF) and TMS-induced changes in functional connectivity for the right FEF (right FEF ROI to left visual cluster r = 0.6, p<0.01; right FEF ROI to right visual cluster r = 0.6, p<0.01)
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between ALFF changes and connectivity changes.

claim: There was a significant correlation between TMS-induced modulation of ALFF and TMS-induced changes in functional connectivity for the right occipital pole (right occipital ROI to left visual cluster r = 0.4, trend-level p=0.05).
source: and for the right occipital pole (right occipital ROI to left visual cluster r = 0.4, trend-level p=0.05) (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between ALFF changes and connectivity changes, with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: Local TMS-induced reductions in neural activity, as indexed by the amplitude of slow fluctuations in the local BOLD signal, were associated with changes in functional connectivity across visual areas.
source: This analysis suggests that local TMS-induced reductions in neural activity, as indexed by the amplitude of slow fluctuations in the local BOLD signal, were associated with changes in functional connectivity across visual areas.
evidence: Interpretation of the correlation analysis results.

claim: Stimulation of V1/V2 altered the feedforward influence of V1/V2 on the right occipito-parietal cortex (paired t-test p=0.04).
source: DCM analyses of model parameters (pre- versus post-TMS) suggested that stimulation of V1/V2 altered the feedforward influence of V1/V2 on the right occipito-parietal cortex (details in Figure 3—figure supplement 5 and Supplementary file 1, paired t-test p=0.04).
evidence: Supported by DCM statistical analysis with reference to supplementary materials.

claim: Stimulation of FEF significantly decreased the feedback influence of this region upon V1/V2 (p=0.0026 for the right cluster and p=0.0012 for the left cluster).
source: Conversely, stimulation of FEF significantly decreased the feedback influence of this region upon V1/V2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 5, p=0.0026 for the right cluster and p=0.0012 for the left cluster).
evidence: Supported by DCM statistical analysis with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: For both V1/V2 and FEF, modulation of effective connectivity induced by focal TMS spread from the stimulation site to distant cortical regions.
source: Thus, for both V1/V2 and FEF, modulation of effective connectivity induced by focal TMS spread from the stimulation site to distant cortical regions.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the DCM analysis results.

claim: Virtual inhibition of right V1/V2 within the computational model increased the positive correlations between this region and the rest of the brain, consistent with the group effects observed following actual TMS.
source: Simulation results showed that virtual inhibition of right V1/V2 within the model increased the positive correlations between this region and the rest of the brain (red in Figure 4a), consistent with the group effects we observed following actual TMS over this region in our participant group.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results compared to experimental data, with reference to Figure 4a.

claim: The simulated effect of local V1/V2 inhibition was due mainly to a significant increase in connectivity between this node and other nodes encompassing occipito-temporal and frontal areas of the right hemisphere.
source: Importantly, we found that the simulated effect of local V1/V2 inhibition was due mainly to a significant increase in connectivity between this node and other nodes encompassing occipito-temporal and frontal areas of the right hemisphere (Figure 4b).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results with reference to Figure 4b.

claim: Simulated inhibition of FEF was associated with the reduction of correlations in this region's connectivity with the rest of the brain.
source: Conversely, simulated inhibition of FEF, again by slowing its intrinsic frequency, was associated with the reduction of correlations in this region's connectivity with the rest of the brain (blue in Figure 4a and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results with reference to Figure 4a and supplementary figure.

claim: Simulated inhibition of FEF involved a significant effect on right frontal areas surrounding FEF, and occipito-temporal cortices.
source: This significant effect involved right frontal areas surrounding FEF, and occipito-temporal cortices (Figure 4c).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results with reference to Figure 4c.

claim: The effects observed within the computational model were consistent with the effects observed following actual TMS of V1/V2 and FEF in the experimental participants.
source: Overall, the effects observed within the model were consistent with the effects observed following actual TMS of V1/V2 and FEF in the experimental participants.
evidence: Comparison between computational model and experimental results.

claim: At baseline, prior to inhibitory stimulation, neural activity in early visual cortex was anticorrelated with activity in the FEF bilaterally.
source: At baseline, prior to inhibitory stimulation, neural activity in early visual cortex was anticorrelated with activity in the FEF bilaterally.
evidence: Summary of baseline connectivity findings.

claim: Previous neuroimaging work in humans and monkey has suggested little or no functional coupling between FEF and V1/V2 in the resting state (Vincent et al., 2007; Belcher et al., 2013; Damoiseaux et al., 2006; Yeo et al., 2011; Power et al., 2011; Mantini et al., 2013; Gordon et al., 2016).
source: Previous neuroimaging work in humans and monkey has suggested little or no functional coupling between FEF and V1/V2 in the resting state (Vincent et al., 2007; Belcher et al., 2013; Damoiseaux et al., 2006; Yeo et al., 2011; Power et al., 2011; Mantini et al., 2013; Gordon et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Areas V1 and V2 lie within a primary visual network that does not include FEF (Yeo et al., 2011).
source: For instance, areas V1 and V2 lie within a primary visual network that does not include FEF (Yeo et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Inhibition of early visual cortex resulted in the emergence of positive correlations between this region and FEF, along with other extrastriate and parietal visual areas.
source: A novel finding of our study is that inhibition of early visual cortex resulted in the emergence of positive correlations between this region and FEF, along with other extrastriate and parietal visual areas.
evidence: Summary of key experimental finding.

claim: Inhibitory TMS of the primary motor cortex in healthy adults has been shown to increase the strength of resting-state functional connectivity within the sensorimotor system (Cocchi et al., 2015).
source: For example, inhibitory TMS of the primary motor cortex in healthy adults has recently been shown to increase the strength of resting-state functional connectivity within the sensorimotor system (Cocchi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Local perturbations of neural activity in peripheral nodes recruit functionally related brain regions (Cocchi et al., 2015; O'Shea et al., 2007; Grefkes and Fink, 2011; Bestmann et al., 2010).
source: Our finding that unilateral inhibition of early visual cortex increases the positive coupling with FEF and other visual areas adds to a growing literature suggesting that local perturbations of neural activity in peripheral nodes recruit functionally related brain regions (Cocchi et al., 2015; O'Shea et al., 2007; Grefkes and Fink, 2011; Bestmann et al., 2010).
evidence: Interpretation of results supported by multiple citations.

claim: The effect of inhibitory TMS of early visual cortex might be due to slowing of intrinsic timescales within V1/V2, so that they become closer to the slow intrinsic fluctuations of higher cortical regions such as the parietal cortex and FEF (Murray et al., 2014; Honey et al., 2012; Gollo et al., 2015; Chaudhuri et al., 2015).
source: Specifically, our computational modelling suggests that the effect of inhibitory TMS of early visual cortex might be due to slowing of intrinsic timescales within V1/V2, so that they become closer to the slow intrinsic fluctuations of higher cortical regions such as the parietal cortex and FEF (Murray et al., 2014; Honey et al., 2012; Gollo et al., 2015; Chaudhuri et al., 2015).
evidence: Mechanistic interpretation based on computational modeling results and supported by citations.

claim: An identical inhibitory TMS protocol delivered over the right FEF led to decoupling between the target region and bilateral early visual cortex.
source: In contrast to the increased positive coupling apparent after inhibition of early visual cortex, an identical inhibitory TMS protocol delivered over the right FEF led to decoupling between the target region and bilateral early visual cortex.
evidence: Summary of key experimental finding contrasting V1/V2 and FEF stimulation effects.

claim: The functional decoupling following FEF stimulation was related to a significant decrease in feedback signals from FEF to early visual cortex.
source: Results from the DCM analysis suggest that such functional decoupling was related to a significant decrease in feedback signals from FEF to early visual cortex.
evidence: Interpretation based on DCM analysis results.

claim: The observed reduction in feedback modulation from FEF to V1/V2 can be explained by a further slowing of local FEF dynamics by TMS.
source: In keeping with the neural mechanism proposed to explain increased connectivity following the inhibition of V1/V2, results from our computational model suggest that the observed reduction in feedback modulation from FEF to V1/V2 can be explained by a further slowing of local FEF dynamics by TMS.
evidence: Mechanistic interpretation based on computational modeling results.

claim: The observed changes in connectivity following inhibitory TMS may be explained in terms of a reduction in synchronization discrepancy following local stimulation of V1/V2 and an increase in synchronization discrepancy following stimulation of FEF.
source: The observed changes in connectivity following inhibitory TMS may therefore be explained in terms of a reduction in synchronization discrepancy following local stimulation of V1/V2 and an increase in synchronization discrepancy following stimulation of FEF.
evidence: Mechanistic interpretation based on computational modeling results.

claim: TMS-induced changes in local BOLD signal amplitude at the stimulation site were related to remote modulations in functional connectivity.
source: Our findings also reveal a relationship between the magnitude of local signal change and remote modulations in intrinsic functional connectivity. We found that TMS-induced changes in local BOLD signal amplitude at the stimulation site were related to remote modulations in functional connectivity.
evidence: Summary of correlation analysis findings.

claim: Variations in ongoing low-frequency (<0.1 Hz) fluctuations may be a marker of TMS-induced modulation of widespread cortical connectivity.
source: This suggests that variations in ongoing low-frequency (<0.1 Hz) fluctuations may be a marker of TMS-induced modulation of widespread cortical connectivity.
evidence: Interpretation of the relationship between ALFF and connectivity changes.

claim: The selective effect of local inhibitory TMS on diffuse patterns of connectivity can be accounted for by an intrinsic hierarchical ordering of cortical timescales (Murray et al., 2014; Honey et al., 2012; Gollo et al., 2015).
source: Our results suggest that the selective effect of local inhibitory TMS on diffuse patterns of connectivity can be accounted for by an intrinsic hierarchical ordering of cortical timescales (Murray et al., 2014; Honey et al., 2012; Gollo et al., 2015).
evidence: Main conclusion of the study supported by citations.

claim: The primate visual system is a hierarchical network of feedforward and feedback connections that supports visual perception, object recognition and selective attention (Gilbert, 2013).
source: The primate visual system is a hierarchical network of feedforward and feedback connections that supports visual perception, object recognition and selective attention (Gilbert, 2013).
evidence: Background statement supported by citation.

claim: At the earliest level of the visual hierarchy, the primary visual cortex receives input from the lateral geniculate nucleus and propagates this information to higher association areas including the posterior parietal cortex, ventral temporal cortex and frontal eye fields (FEF) (Hubel and Wiesel, 1962; Felleman and Van Essen, 1991; Van Essen and Maunsell, 1983; Maunsell and van Essen, 1983).
source: At the earliest level of the visual hierarchy, the primary visual cortex receives input from the lateral geniculate nucleus and propagates this information to higher association areas including the posterior parietal cortex, ventral temporal cortex and frontal eye fields (FEF) (Hubel and Wiesel, 1962; Felleman and Van Essen, 1991; Van Essen and Maunsell, 1983; Maunsell and van Essen, 1983).
evidence: Background statement supported by multiple citations.

claim: During active perception, neural signals originating in later cortical areas provide top-down modulation of activity in early visual areas, depending on factors such as expectation and context (Gilbert, 2013; Felleman and Van Essen, 1991; Moore and Armstrong, 2003; Bastos et al., 2015).
source: During active perception, neural signals originating in these later cortical areas provide top-down modulation of activity in early visual areas, depending on factors such as expectation and context (Gilbert, 2013; Felleman and Van Essen, 1991; Moore and Armstrong, 2003; Bastos et al., 2015).
evidence: Background statement supported by multiple citations.

claim: Task demands play an important role in determining the nature of the interactions between early and late visual cortex (Gilbert, 2013).
source: This work has demonstrated that task demands play an important role in determining the nature of the interactions between early and late visual cortex (Gilbert, 2013).
evidence: Background statement supported by citation.

claim: Stimulation of the FEF can modulate neural activity in several visual areas, including the primary visual cortex (area V1) (Bressler et al., 2008; Ruff et al., 2006, 2008).
source: For example, studies combining fMRI with transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) during performance of visual tasks have shown that stimulation of the FEF can modulate neural activity in several visual areas, including the primary visual cortex (area V1) (Bressler et al., 2008; Ruff et al., 2006, 2008).
evidence: Background statement supported by multiple citations.

claim: Increments in the strength of excitatory TMS over the right FEF increase neural activity in early retinotopic cortex representing the peripheral visual field, and reduce activity in central visual-field representations (Ruff et al., 2006).
source: Increments in the strength of excitatory TMS over the right FEF have been shown to increase neural activity in early retinotopic cortex representing the peripheral visual field, and to reduce activity in central visual-field representations (Ruff et al., 2006).
evidence: Background statement supported by citation.

claim: This neurophysiological effect confers a perceptual advantage for detection of stimuli in the visual periphery relative to the fovea (Ruff et al., 2006).
source: This neurophysiological effect confers a perceptual advantage for detection of stimuli in the visual periphery relative to the fovea (Ruff et al., 2006).
evidence: Background statement supported by citation.

claim: At rest, FEF belongs to extensive networks of fronto-parietal regions (Yeo et al., 2011; Power et al., 2011).
source: At rest, FEF belongs to extensive networks of fronto-parietal regions (Yeo et al., 2011; Power et al., 2011)
evidence: Background statement supported by citations.

claim: The early visual cortex, including area V1, belongs to a primary visual network encompassing occipital and inferior parietal regions (Yeo et al., 2011; Power et al., 2011; Gordon et al., 2016).
source: whereas the early visual cortex, including area V1, belongs to a primary visual network encompassing occipital and inferior parietal regions (Yeo et al., 2011; Power et al., 2011; Gordon et al., 2016).
evidence: Background statement supported by multiple citations.

claim: The study was approved by The University of Queensland Human Research Ethics Committee.
source: The study was approved by The University of Queensland Human Research Ethics Committee.
evidence: Directly states ethical approval.

claim: Written informed consent was obtained for all participants.
source: Written informed consent was obtained for all participants.
evidence: Directly states consent procedure.

claim: Target regions for inhibitory theta-burst TMS were defined using high-resolution structural T1 3D images obtained for each participant and loaded into an ANT Visor Neuro-navigation system with NDI Polaris Spectra infrared camera.
source: Target regions for inhibitory theta-burst TMS were defined using high-resolution structural T1 3D images obtained for each participant and loaded into an ANT Visor Neuro-navigation system with NDI Polaris Spectra infrared camera.
evidence: Describes the method for defining TMS targets.

claim: The two TMS target sites were identified prior to the first experimental session.
source: The two TMS target sites were identified prior to the first experimental session (Figure 1).
evidence: Describes the timing of target identification with reference to Figure 1.

claim: The anatomical locations of the TMS target coordinates were manually refined according to each individual participant's anatomy.
source: The anatomical locations of the TMS target coordinates were manually refined according to each individual participant's anatomy.
evidence: Describes the individualization procedure for TMS targets.

claim: If the target region was located in a sulcus, the location for TMS was moved to the gyrus closest to the centroid coordinate.
source: Specifically, if the target region was located in a sulcus, the location for TMS was moved to the gyrus closest to the centroid coordinate (V1/V2: MNI centroid x = 25, y = −92, z = −9; FEF: MNI centroid x = 31 y = −2, z = 47).
evidence: Describes the adjustment procedure for TMS target placement.

claim: The early visual cortex target was located anatomically within the occipital pole, posterior to the descending occipital gyrus laterally and the lingual gyrus medially (corresponding to areas V1/V2 [Thiebaut de Schotten et al., 2014]).
source: The early visual cortex target was located anatomically within the occipital pole, posterior to the descending occipital gyrus laterally and the lingual gyrus medially (corresponding to areas V1/V2 [Thiebaut de Schotten et al., 2014]).
evidence: Describes anatomical location with citation.

claim: The FEF target was located anatomically within the posterior middle frontal gyrus, immediately ventral to the junction of the superior frontal sulcus and ascending limb of the pre-central sulcus (Ruff et al., 2006; Heinen et al., 2014).
source: In line with previous studies, the FEF target was located anatomically within the posterior middle frontal gyrus, immediately ventral to the junction of the superior frontal sulcus and ascending limb of the pre-central sulcus (Ruff et al., 2006; Heinen et al., 2014).
evidence: Describes anatomical location with citations to prior studies.

claim: A continuous theta-burst TMS protocol was utilized to induce local inhibition of cortical activity using a previously validated protocol (Huang et al., 2005).
source: A continuous theta-burst TMS protocol was utilized to induce local inhibition of cortical activity using a previously validated protocol (Huang et al., 2005).
evidence: Describes the TMS protocol with citation.

claim: The inhibitory TMS protocol involved uninterrupted (40 seconds) bursts of 3 TMS pulses delivered at 50 Hz, repeated at 200 ms intervals.
source: The inhibitory TMS protocol involved uninterrupted (40 seconds) bursts of 3 TMS pulses delivered at 50 Hz, repeated at 200 ms intervals.
evidence: Describes the specific parameters of the TMS protocol.

claim: TMS was administered using a figure-of-eight coil (70 mm diameter).
source: TMS was administered using a figure-of-eight coil (70 mm diameter).
evidence: Describes the TMS equipment.

claim: For FEF stimulation, the TMS coil handle was held at a 45-degree angle to the sagittal plane (Nyffeler et al., 2006).
source: For FEF stimulation, the TMS coil handle was held at a 45-degree angle to the sagittal plane (Nyffeler et al., 2006).
evidence: Describes coil orientation with citation.

claim: For stimulation of the right occipital pole, the coil was oriented with the handle pointing to the right (Kammer et al., 2001).
source: For stimulation of the right occipital pole, the coil was oriented with the handle pointing to the right (Kammer et al., 2001).
evidence: Describes coil orientation with citation.

claim: The intensity of the inhibitory stimulation of the two cortical ROIs was set to 80% of the active motor threshold (Huang et al., 2005; Cocchi et al., 2015).
source: The intensity of the inhibitory stimulation of the two cortical ROIs was set to 80% of the active motor threshold (Huang et al., 2005; Cocchi et al., 2015).
evidence: Describes TMS intensity with citations.

claim: The active motor threshold was defined as the minimum TMS intensity required to trigger a motor evoked potential (MEP) > 200 µV in at least three out of five consecutive trials while participants were actively contracting their hand muscle at a level equivalent to ~20% of their maximum voluntary contraction (Huang et al., 2005).
source: The active motor threshold was defined as the minimum TMS intensity required to trigger a motor evoked potential (MEP) > 200 µV in at least three out of five consecutive trials while participants were actively contracting their hand muscle (using a pincer grip) at a level equivalent to ~20% of their maximum voluntary contraction (Huang et al., 2005).
evidence: Describes the method for determining motor threshold with citation.

claim: During resting state fMRI scans, participants were instructed to keep their eyes open and to fixate on a central white cross on a uniform black background.
source: During resting state fMRI scans, participants were instructed to keep their eyes open and to fixate on a central white cross on a uniform black background.
evidence: Describes the resting-state scan instructions.

claim: Participants were instructed to let their minds wander freely during the scan.
source: Participants were instructed to let their minds wander freely during the scan.
evidence: Describes the resting-state scan instructions.

claim: Eye tracking video software was employed to ensure that participants kept their eyes open and looked straight ahead throughout the sessions of resting-state fMRI data acquisition.
source: Eye tracking video software was employed to ensure that participants kept their eyes open and looked straight ahead throughout the sessions of resting-state fMRI data acquisition.
evidence: Describes the monitoring procedure during scans.

claim: The eye-open resting-state protocol was preferred over the eye-closed protocol due to recent concerns about controlling wakefulness when participants have their eyes closed (Tagliazucchi and Laufs, 2014).
source: The eye-open resting-state protocol was preferred over the eye-closed protocol due to recent concerns about controlling wakefulness when participants have their eyes closed (Tagliazucchi and Laufs, 2014).
evidence: Justifies the choice of eyes-open protocol with citation.

claim: Neuroimaging data were acquired using a 3T Siemens Trio scanner equipped with a 32-channel head coil at The University of Queensland's Centre for Advanced Imaging (Australia).
source: Neuroimaging data were acquired using a 3T Siemens Trio scanner equipped with a 32-channel head coil at The University of Queensland's Centre for Advanced Imaging (Australia).
evidence: Describes the MRI scanner and location.

claim: Whole brain T2* images were acquired using an echo-planar imaging sequence (38 axial slices, 320 volumes, gap = 10%, slice thickness = 3 mm, in-plane resolution = 64 × 64, time repetition = 2250 ms, time echo = 28 ms, flip angle = 90°, FOV= 210 × 210 mm, descending slice acquisition).
source: Whole brain T2* images were acquired using an echo-planar imaging sequence (38 axial slices, 320 volumes, gap = 10%, slice thickness = 3 mm, in-plane resolution = 64 × 64, time repetition = 2250 ms, time echo = 28 ms, flip angle = 90°, FOV= 210 × 210 mm, descending slice acquisition).
evidence: Describes the functional imaging parameters.

claim: T1 3D images were acquired using the following parameters: 192 axial slices, slice thickness = 0.9 mm; in-plane resolution = 64 × 64, time repetition = 1900 ms, flip angle= 9°, time echo = 2.32 ms, FOV = 230 × 230 mm.
source: T1 3D images were acquired using the following parameters: 192 axial slices, slice thickness = 0.9 mm; in-plane resolution = 64 × 64, time repetition = 1900 ms, flip angle= 9°, time echo = 2.32 ms, FOV = 230 × 230 mm.
evidence: Describes the structural imaging parameters.

claim: Preprocessing of the resting-state fMRI data was performed using the Data Processing Assistant for Resting-State fMRI 3 (Chao-Gan and Yu-Feng, 2010).
source: Preprocessing of the resting-state fMRI data was performed using the Data Processing Assistant for Resting-State fMRI 3 (Chao-Gan and Yu-Feng, 2010).
evidence: Describes the preprocessing software with citation.

claim: The first 10 image volumes were discarded to allow tissue magnetization to reach a steady-state and to provide participants with an opportunity to adapt to the MR scanner environment.
source: The first 10 image volumes were discarded to allow tissue magnetization to reach a steady-state and to provide participants with an opportunity to adapt to the MR scanner environment.
evidence: Describes a preprocessing step with rationale.

claim: Individual participant structural images (T1) were coregistered to functional images using the DARTEL algorithm implemented within the Matlab toolbox SPM8.
source: To improve normalization, individual participant structural images (T1) were coregistered to functional images using the DARTEL algorithm implemented within the Matlab toolbox SPM8.
evidence: Describes a preprocessing step.

claim: Tissue segmentation (gray matter, white matter and cerebrospinal fluid) was performed to improve the characterization of non-neural signals in subject space.
source: Tissue segmentation (gray matter, white matter and cerebrospinal fluid) was performed to improve the characterization of non-neural signals in subject space.
evidence: Describes a preprocessing step with rationale.

claim: Nuisance covariates regressed from each voxel's time series included: six head motion parameters, linear trends, volume-level mean of frame-to-frame displacements greater than 0.4 mm (including the preceding and two subsequent frames [Power et al., 2014]) and signals related to time-series unlikely to be modulated by neural activity (CompCor method [Behzadi et al., 2007]).
source: The following nuisance covariates were regressed from each voxel's time series: six head motion parameters, linear trends, volume-level mean of frame-to-frame displacements greater than 0.4 mm (including the preceding and two subsequent frames [Power et al., 2014]) and signals related to time-series unlikely to be modulated by neural activity (CompCor method [Behzadi et al., 2007]).
evidence: Describes preprocessing steps with citations.

claim: After covariate regression, images were normalized to standard MNI space, smoothed using a Gaussian function with a 6 mm full width at half maximum kernel.
source: After covariate regression, images were normalized to standard MNI space, smoothed using a Gaussian function with a 6 mm full width at half maximum kernel.
evidence: Describes preprocessing steps.

claim: A temporal bandpass filter was applied retaining frequencies between 0.01–0.1 Hz.
source: Finally, a temporal bandpass filter was applied retaining frequencies between 0.01–0.1 Hz.
evidence: Describes a preprocessing step.

claim: Both the mean frame-wise displacement and the number of scrubbed volumes were not significantly different for the pre- and post-TMS scans, in either experimental session.
source: Supplementary analyses demonstrated that both the mean frame-wise displacement (Power et al., 2014) and the number of scrubbed volumes were not significantly different for the pre- and post-TMS scans, in either experimental session.
evidence: Reports results of motion analysis with citation.

claim: After scrubbing motion-contaminated volumes, the number of remaining volumes for each functional scanning session exceeded 8.8 min, which is sufficient time to capture stable correlation coefficients (Van Dijk et al., 2010).
source: Note that after scrubbing motion-contaminated volumes (Power et al., 2014), the number of remaining volumes for each functional scanning session exceeded 8.8 min, which is sufficient time to capture stable correlation coefficients (Van Dijk et al., 2010).
evidence: Reports data quality metric with citations.

claim: Global signal regression was not performed during pre-processing due to recent concerns in the literature.
source: Given recent concerns in the literature regarding the use of global signal regression, we did not regress the mean global signal during pre-processing.
evidence: Describes a methodological decision with rationale.

claim: The mean global signal was not significantly different across pre- and post-TMS sessions, for either stimulation site (occipital TMS session: t20 = 1.22, p=0.23, FEF TMS session: t20 = 0.941, p=0.35).
source: The mean global signal was not significantly different across pre- and post-TMS sessions, for either stimulation site (occipital TMS session: t20 = 1.22, p=0.23, FEF TMS session: t20 = 0.941, p=0.35).
evidence: Reports statistical test results.

claim: Re-running the analysis incorporating regression of the mean BOLD signal obtained similar results.
source: Nevertheless, to ensure that this methodological decision did not alter the main results reported here, we re-ran the analysis incorporating regression of the mean BOLD signal, and obtained similar results.
evidence: Reports results of control analysis.

claim: Seed-to-voxel correlation analyses were conducted to examine patterns of functional connectivity between seed ROIs (TMS target sites) with voxels in the rest of the brain.
source: Seed-to-voxel correlation analyses were conducted to examine patterns of functional connectivity between seed ROIs (TMS target sites) with voxels in the rest of the brain.
evidence: Describes the analysis method.

claim: Mean timeseries were extracted across grey matter voxels within a quasi-spherical grey matter seed (radius ~7.5 mm) centered on the group-level coordinates in the right occipital pole (MNI centroid x = 25, y = −92, z = −9) and right FEF (MNI centroid x = 31 y = −2, z = 47).
source: We first extracted the mean timeseries across grey matter voxels within a quasi-spherical grey matter seed (radius ~7.5 mm) centered on the group-level coordinates in the right occipital pole (MNI centroid x = 25, y = −92, z = −9) and right FEF (MNI centroid x = 31 y = −2, z = 47).
evidence: Describes the seed definition for connectivity analysis.

claim: All results presented in the main text were obtained using grey matter ROIs with a radius of 7.5 mm.
source: Note that all of the results presented in the main text were obtained using the grey matter ROIs with a radius of 7.5 mm.
evidence: Clarifies the ROI size used for main analyses.

claim: The main findings were replicated using additional ROIs with radii of 10 mm and 15 mm.
source: While this ROI dimension was found to best encompass the participants' targeted brain areas in standard MNI space, the main findings were also replicated using additional ROIs with radii of 10 mm and 15 mm; see Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.
evidence: Reports replication of results with different ROI sizes, with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: Seed-to-voxel analysis enabled the generation of subject-level spatial maps representing correlation coefficients between the targeted seed with each individual brain voxel for both pre- and post-TMS sessions.
source: We then conducted a seed-to-voxel analysis, whereby the mean timeseries extracted within each seed ROI was correlated with the timeseries extracted from each voxel in the rest of the brain. This analysis enabled the generation of subject-level spatial maps representing correlation coefficients between the targeted seed with each individual brain voxel for both pre- and post-TMS sessions.
evidence: Describes the connectivity analysis procedure.

claim: The resulting correlation coefficients were Z-transformed to improve the application of univariate second-level statistics.
source: The resulting correlation coefficients were Z-transformed to improve the application of univariate second-level statistics.
evidence: Describes a statistical transformation step.

claim: Seed-to-voxel functional connectivity was calculated at baseline (session specific) using one-sample t-tests, for both experimental sessions (V1/V2 and FEF, FWE corrected threshold of p<0.05 at the cluster level).
source: Seed-to-voxel functional connectivity was calculated at baseline (session specific) using one-sample t-tests, for both experimental sessions (V1/V2 and FEF, FWE corrected threshold of p<0.05 at the cluster level, Figure 2).
evidence: Describes the statistical analysis for baseline connectivity with reference to Figure 2.

claim: Seed-to-voxel functional connectivity was compared across the pre- and post-TMS scans using paired-sample t-tests, for both resting-state fMRI sessions (V1/V2 and FEF, FWE corrected threshold of p<0.05 at the cluster level).
source: Seed-to-voxel functional connectivity was compared across the pre (session specific)- and post-TMS scans using paired-sample t-tests, for both resting-state fMRI sessions (V1/V2 and FEF, FWE corrected threshold of p<0.05 at the cluster level, Figure 3).
evidence: Describes the statistical analysis for TMS effects with reference to Figure 3.

claim: The amplitude of low frequency fluctuations (ALFF, 0.01–0.1 Hz) was extracted from each ROI for each individual participant, for both the pre- and post-TMS scanning sessions.
source: The amplitude of low frequency fluctuations (Yang et al., 2007) (ALFF, 0.01–0.1 Hz) was extracted from each ROI for each individual participant, for both the pre- and post-TMS scanning sessions.
evidence: Describes the ALFF analysis with citation.

claim: TMS-induced change in ALFF was correlated with TMS-induced changes in functional connectivity between the target seed and the significant group level clusters using bivariate Pearson's correlations.
source: We then correlated the TMS-induced change in ALFF with the TMS-induced changes in functional connectivity between the target seed and the significant group level clusters identified in the previous analysis (see Neuroimaging analysis: Seed-to-voxel analysis) using bivariate Pearson's correlations.
evidence: Describes the correlation analysis between ALFF and connectivity changes.

claim: Effects of TMS stimulation on effective connectivity were analyzed using stochastic DCM implemented in DCM12 (Daunizeau et al., 2012).
source: Effects of TMS stimulation on effective connectivity were analyzed using stochastic DCM implemented in DCM12 (Daunizeau et al., 2012).
evidence: Describes the DCM analysis method with citation.

claim: DCM is a computational framework for inferring effective connectivity between cortical regions.
source: DCM is a computational framework for inferring effective connectivity between cortical regions.
evidence: Defines DCM.

claim: Model estimation in DCM rests on the Bayesian inversion of state space models by combining dynamic models of neural states with biophysical models of hemodynamics (Friston et al., 2014).
source: Model estimation rests on the Bayesian inversion of state space models by combining dynamic models of neural states with biophysical models of hemodynamics (Friston et al., 2014).
evidence: Describes DCM methodology with citation.

claim: Stochastic DCM allows inverting models with uncertainty about the temporal specification of inputs.
source: Importantly, stochastic DCM allows inverting models with uncertainty about the temporal specification of inputs.
evidence: Describes a feature of stochastic DCM.

claim: Stochastic DCM is particularly useful for model inversion of resting-state data (Stephan et al., 2010).
source: Because these inputs can represent intrinsic fluctuations, stochastic DCM is particularly useful for model inversion of resting-state data (Stephan et al., 2010).
evidence: Justifies use of stochastic DCM with citation.

claim: For each participant, timeseries were extracted from regions of interest defined by the seed-to-voxel analysis of functional connectivity.
source: For each participant, timeseries were extracted from regions of interest defined by the seed-to-voxel analysis of functional connectivity (Figure 3).
evidence: Describes the DCM analysis procedure with reference to Figure 3.

claim: For both stimulation sessions, a 7.5 mm spherical seed was used on targeted regions and main clusters showing a significant TMS effect.
source: For both stimulation sessions (Figure 1) we used a 7.5 mm spherical seed on targeted regions and main clusters showing a significant TMS effect (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Describes the seed definition for DCM with references to figures.

claim: Two distinct DCM models were created (one for each session) with bidirectional connections between the respective TMS target region (V1/V2 or FEF) and the selected clusters.
source: This resulted in two distinct models (one for each session) with bidirectional connections between the respective TMS target region (V1/V2 or FEF) and the selected clusters.
evidence: Describes the DCM model structure.

claim: The DCM models were inverted to estimate subject-specific parameters.
source: The models were subsequently inverted to estimate subject-specific parameters.
evidence: Describes the DCM analysis procedure.

claim: At the group level, the DCM model parameters between the pre- and post-TMS brain states were compared using pairwise two-tailed t-statistics.
source: At the group level, the model parameters between the pre- and post-TMS brain states were compared using pairwise two-tailed t-statistics.
evidence: Describes the statistical analysis of DCM parameters.

claim: The Kuramoto model was utilized as a minimal and standard computational model of synchronization (Kuramoto, 1984).
source: We utilized a minimal and standard computational model of synchronization (Kuramoto, 1984).
evidence: Describes the computational model with citation.

claim: The Kuramoto model was chosen because it captures the same essential aspects of macroscopic dynamics as more complex models (Bhowmik and Shanahan, 2013).
source: In line with previous work (Hellyer et al., 2015), we chose this model because it captures the same essential aspects of macroscopic dynamics as more complex models (Bhowmik and Shanahan, 2013).
evidence: Justifies model choice with citations.

claim: The Kuramoto model provides a good trade-off between complexity and plausibility, incorporating key anatomical constraints and modelling functional elements (Hellyer et al., 2015).
source: The Kuramoto model thus provides a good trade-off between complexity and plausibility, incorporating key anatomical constraints and modelling functional elements (Hellyer et al., 2015).
evidence: Justifies model choice with citation.

claim: The Kuramoto model is particularly suitable to assess signal correlations between distinct network nodes and is capable of reproducing the experimental results.
source: This model is particularly suitable to assess signal correlations between distinct network nodes and, importantly, is capable of reproducing our experimental results.
evidence: Justifies model choice based on its capabilities.

claim: In the Kuramoto model, the local effect of inhibitory TMS can be represented by reducing a single parameter.
source: The model yields a simulation of whole-brain dynamics in which the (consistent) local effect of inhibitory TMS can be represented by reducing a single parameter, as described in detail below.
evidence: Describes how TMS is modeled.

claim: Slow (0.01–0.1 Hz) fluctuations of the BOLD signal in 513 volumetrically similar brain regions were modelled as oscillators.
source: We modelled slow (0.01–0.1 Hz) fluctuations of the BOLD signal in 513 volumetrically similar brain regions (Zalesky et al., 2010) as oscillators.
evidence: Describes the modeling approach with citation.

claim: Fast and slow cortical oscillations can be modelled with systems of coupled phase oscillators as encompassed within the Kuramoto model (Breakspear et al., 2010; Schmidt et al., 2015).
source: Fast (Breakspear et al., 2010) and slow (Schmidt et al., 2015) cortical oscillations can be modelled with systems of coupled phase oscillators as encompassed within the Kuramoto model.
evidence: Justifies modeling approach with citations.

claim: The representative connectivity matrix W used in the Kuramoto model was obtained from a sample of 75 healthy adult participants (Roberts et al., 2016).
source: The representative connectivity matrix W used in the Kuramoto model – Equation (1) – was obtained from a sample of 75 healthy adult participants (Roberts et al., 2016).
evidence: Describes the source of anatomical connectivity data with citation.

claim: Probabilistic tractography was used to estimate the average number of white matter tracks connecting all pairs of brain regions (513 x 512= 262,656 connections).
source: Probabilistic tractography was used to estimate the average number of white matter tracks connecting all pairs of brain regions (513 x 512= 262,656 connections; details in Roberts et al. [Roberts et al., 2016]).
evidence: Describes the method for obtaining structural connectivity with citation.

claim: The structural connectivity matrix was normalized.
source: The resulting structural connectivity matrix was normalized.
evidence: Describes a processing step for the connectivity matrix.

claim: The model was run using a sparser structural connectivity matrix (30% density vs. original densely connected matrix) to ensure robustness to possible inaccuracies in streamline reconstruction.
source: To ensure that the findings of our model were robust to possible inaccuracies in streamline reconstruction, however, we ran the model using (i) a sparser structural connectivity matrix (30% density vs. original densely connected matrix)
evidence: Describes a control analysis.

claim: The model was run with a correction for the reconstruction of long-range connections (division of the original weights by the fiber distance between any two regions).
source: and (ii) a correction for the reconstruction of long-range connections (division of the original weights by the fiber distance between any two regions).
evidence: Describes a control analysis.

claim: Control analyses replicated the original result showing that TMS of FEF increases the discrepancy between activity in this brain region and V1/V2, whereas TMS of V1/V2 decreases the discrepancy.
source: These analyses replicated the original result showing that TMS of FEF increases the discrepancy between activity in this brain region and V1/V2, whereas TMS of V1/V2 decreases the discrepancy.
evidence: Reports results of control analyses.

claim: The robustness of the model results is largely explained by the fact that FEF consistently has a high degree (i.e., is a hub) whereas V1/V2 is consistently a peripheral node with a comparatively low degree.
source: This robustness is largely explained by the fact that FEF consistently has a high degree (i.e., is a hub) whereas V1/V2 is consistently a peripheral node with a comparatively low degree.
evidence: Provides an explanation for the robustness of model results.

claim: The model was calibrated (varying λ) to closely match the baseline functional connectivity of the two stimulated regions with the rest of the brain using the 513-region brain parcellation.
source: We started by calibrating the model (varying λ) to closely match the baseline functional connectivity of the two stimulated regions (i.e., the network state prior to application of TMS) with the rest of the brain using the 513-region brain parcellation.
evidence: Describes the model calibration procedure.

claim: Single-subject 513 x 513 connectivity matrices were calculated using the previously preprocessed data.
source: To this end, we calculated single-subject 513 x 513 connectivity matrices using the previously preprocessed data (see Preprocessing of neuroimaging data section for details).
evidence: Describes the data used for model calibration.

claim: 500 simulations were performed for a period of 8 min (discarding 2.12 min of transient time) using the model with random initial conditions for varying λ values.
source: We then performed 500 simulations for a period of 8 min (discarding 2.12 min of transient time) using the aforementioned model with random initial conditions for varying λ values.
evidence: Describes the simulation parameters.

claim: λ was selected and fixed at 0.0028 for consistency.
source: We then selected and fixed λ (=0.0028) for consistency, and verified that small variations did not unduly affect the dynamics.
evidence: Describes the parameter selection.

claim: The simulated trials that best replicated the functional connectivity in the real data were selected for each participant.
source: The simulated trials that best replicated the functional connectivity in the real data were selected for each participant.
evidence: Describes the trial selection procedure.

claim: The final correlation between data and simulations for the average functional connectivity between V1/V2 and the rest of the brain was r = 0.55.
source: The final correlation between data and simulations for the average functional connectivity between V1/V2 (FEF) and the rest of the brain was r = 0.55 (0.45).
evidence: Reports the model fit for V1/V2.

claim: The final correlation between data and simulations for the average functional connectivity between FEF and the rest of the brain was r = 0.45.
source: The final correlation between data and simulations for the average functional connectivity between V1/V2 (FEF) and the rest of the brain was r = 0.55 (0.45).
evidence: Reports the model fit for FEF.

claim: To mimic the putative effect of inhibitory TMS on local oscillations, numerous simulations (500 trials) were run with reductions in ω spanning from 10–5 to 10–2 Hz (for both V1/V2 and FEF) (Wozniak-Kwasniewska et al., 2014).
source: To mimic the putative effect of inhibitory TMS on local oscillations (Wozniak-Kwasniewska et al., 2014) we ran numerous simulations (500 trials) with reductions in ω spanning from 10–5 to 10–2 Hz (for both V1/V2 and FEF).
evidence: Describes the simulation of TMS effects with citation.

claim: The simulations reproduced the topology of changes in functional connectivity between the two stimulation sites and the rest of the brain that were obtained following application of TMS in the participant group.
source: These simulations reproduced the topology of changes in functional connectivity between the two stimulation sites – V1/V2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 4a) and FEF (Figure 4—figure supplement 4b) – and the rest of the brain that were obtained following application of TMS in the participant group.
evidence: Reports that simulations matched experimental results with references to supplementary figures.

claim: The average change in functional connectivity between V1/V2 and FEF and the rest of the brain was quantified, and regions showing statistically significant changes were identified (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, Bonferroni corrected for multiple comparisons).
source: We then quantified the average change in functional connectivity between these regions and the rest of the brain, and identified regions in which the changes in functional connectivity were statistically significant (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, Bonferroni corrected for multiple comparisons).
evidence: Describes the statistical analysis of simulation results.

claim: Local inhibition of early visual cortex reduces the discrepancy in endogenous synchronization between lower and higher levels of the visual cortical hierarchy.
source: Our experimental and modelling results suggest that local inhibition of early visual cortex reduces the discrepancy in endogenous synchronization between lower and higher levels of the visual cortical hierarchy
evidence: Main conclusion from experimental and modeling results.

claim: Inhibition of FEF increases the discrepancy in endogenous synchronization between lower and higher levels of the visual cortical hierarchy.
source: whereas inhibition of FEF increases the discrepancy.
evidence: Main conclusion from experimental and modeling results.

claim: The work provides novel insights into the neural mechanisms that underlie the effects of local inhibition on large-scale brain dynamics.
source: Our work provides novel insights into the neural mechanisms that underlie the effects of local inhibition on large-scale brain dynamics.
evidence: Summary statement of the study's contribution.

claim: Stimulation of early visual cortex selectively increased feedforward interactions with FEF and extrastriate visual areas.
source: We found that stimulation of early visual cortex selectively increased feedforward interactions with FEF and extrastriate visual areas
evidence: Summary of key finding from the Abstract.

claim: Identical stimulation of the FEF decreased feedback interactions with early visual areas.
source: whereas identical stimulation of the FEF decreased feedback interactions with early visual areas.
evidence: Summary of key finding from the Abstract.

claim: These opposing effects reflect a fast-slow timescale hierarchy from sensory to association areas.
source: Computational modelling suggests that these opposing effects reflect a fast-slow timescale hierarchy from sensory to association areas.
evidence: Main conclusion from computational modeling stated in the Abstract.
